prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue aspirin alongside the anticoagulant in the absence of a separate coronary indication
Do not confine management to risk-factor control as for small-vessel disease when atrial fibrillation is documented
Do not withhold anticoagulation because of age or cognitive impairment alone [ESC_AF_2024]
Do not refer for carotid revascularisation for a 30-40% stenosis
Do not prescribe strongly anticholinergic drugs
required_recommendations: Start a DOAC for atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VA 5: age 76, hypertension, prior stroke), e.g. apixaban 5 mg twice daily (no dose-reduction criterion: age under 80, weight 82 kg, creatinine 1.12 mg/dL), and stop aspirin [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary]
Lower blood pressure (146/82 mmHg) gradually to below 130/80 mmHg, checking orthostatic BP at each change [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary]

Intensify lipid lowering from simvastatin 40 mg to a high-intensity statin, aiming at LDL below 55 mg/dL (current 122 mg/dL): very high risk after ischaemic strokes at 76 with hypertension and carotid atherosclerosis; add ezetimibe if the goal is not reached [ACC_AHA_dyslipidemia_2026]
Advise reducing alcohol (two glasses of wine daily), which adds to bleeding risk on anticoagulation and to cognitive impairment
Confirm that he does not resume driving, and provide caregiver support and a plan for the finances his wife has taken over

avoided_actions.rationale: No rapidly progressive or fluctuating course and no episodes suggesting seizures; EEG has no diagnostic role in this stepwise decline.
No parkinsonism, fluctuations, hallucinations or dream enactment; a dopamine transporter scan does not address the vascular question.
No feature of Lewy body disease or autonomic failure; cardiac sympathetic imaging does not inform this diagnosis.
A chronic stepwise decline dated to two focal events, not a subacute multidomain syndrome: an untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune battery has no indication.
MRI is available and not contraindicated; CT cannot show microbleeds, siderosis or small lacunes.
Atrial fibrillation is present on the 12-lead ECG; prolonged monitoring does not change the indication for anticoagulation.

accepted: Vascular dementia: multi-infarct type, cardioembolic, secondary to previously undocumented atrial fibrillation
major neurocognitive disorder due to vascular disease

differential.key_features: The course is stepwise with dateable events, recall is cue-responsive, medial temporal lobes are preserved, and three cortical infarcts in three territories and a caudate lacune account for the deficit
The white matter burden is only Fazekas 1, far below the threshold at which small-vessel disease can be held responsible for a dementia
Carotid stenosis is 30-40% on the right and under 30% on the left, non-flow-limiting, and cannot produce infarcts in three separate territories including a posterior one
No hippocampal atrophy and no clinical feature of a second degenerative process; the infarct load is sufficient on its own
No fluctuation, hallucinations, parkinsonism or dream enactment

key_clinical_evidence: The distribution of infarction identifies the mechanism: chronic cortical infarcts in three arterial territories in both hemispheres point to a proximal embolic source, not to small-vessel disease or to a single stenosed artery
A Fazekas 1 white matter burden is far below the confluent burden needed to attribute a dementia to small-vessel disease
The irregularly irregular pulse at the bedside and the ECG that followed change management from antiplatelet to anticoagulant therapy

Absolute cognitive scores understate decline from a superior premorbid baseline; a MoCA of 20 in a career accountant is a large fall, and loss of the accounts and driving marks a major (dementia-level) disorder
Once atrial fibrillation is documented, prolonged monitoring adds cost without changing the diagnosis or the treatment

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A 30-40% non-flow-limiting stenosis is below any revascularisation threshold and cannot cause infarcts in three territories including a posterior one; it is a marker of atherosclerosis, not the mechanism
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests a large-artery atherosclerotic mechanism and a revascularisation referral

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Fazekas 1 punctate change is age-expected and far below the confluent burden required to attribute a dementia to small-vessel disease; the multi-territory infarcts are the explanation
red_herrings.intended_effect: Invites a diagnosis of subcortical small-vessel vascular dementia

sequence_constraints.reason: Document the cognitive deficit before attributing it: imaging read without a cognitive profile invites over-attribution of incidental white matter change.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Enrico Salvi is a 76-year-old retired accountant who attends with his wife. She dates his decline to two events. Four years ago he woke with weakness of the right arm and leg that lasted three days and then resolved; he refused hospital assessment and no imaging was obtained. In the months after it he stopped preparing the family tax returns, which he had done for forty years. Two years ago he had a morning of muddled speech, again resolving within a day, and after it he began to lose track of appointments and to repeat himself. Between the events he was stable. Six months ago he became lost driving to his daughter's house, a route he had driven weekly for twenty years, and has not driven since. His wife notes that he remembers events when reminded of their context, and that his difficulty is with planning, sequencing and multitasking. He denies headache, seizures, hallucinations, fluctuation in alertness and dream enactment. At the bedside his pulse is irregularly irregular; he has never been told he has an irregular heartbeat, and his last recorded ECG was eleven years ago.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and cooperative; oriented to person and place, year correct, date incorrect. Slow to plan and sequence answers; conversation coherent, with occasional word-finding pauses for low-frequency words. No neglect. Formal cognitive screening reported separately.
